speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
As hon. members are aware, informal meetings were held in London last week among representatives of Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States to consider various problems arising from international trade in textiles. Officials from the crown colony of Hong Kong were also present. It will be recalled that these meetings followed an announcement by President Kennedy of the United States that a conference of the principal textile importing and exporting countries would be called for the purpose of seeking an international understanding in this field which would provide a basis for expanding trade without undue disruption of established industries. The London discussions were the first of a series of consultations in preparation for a broader international conference.
I have now received a report from the Canadian representatives at these meetings, and can report to the house that encouraging progress was made. It was recognized that the problems which have arisen in the field of textiles could best be dealt with on the basis of a comprehensive international understanding. The countries represented at the London meetings pledged their co-operation in seeking such an international solution. Further consultations will now go forward in order to obtain the views of other principal textile importers and exporters and also to seek the co-operation of the GATT and the O.E.C.D.
Hon. members will appreciate that in a matter of this importance and complexity there exist many diverse interests and views. Accordingly, it was agreed that, consistent with maximum efforts for an early solution, great care should be taken to prepare the ground before convening a formal international conference. It is expected that after
this round of consultations has been completed arrangements will be made for a ministerial meeting in the latter part of June.
I should like to assure the house that Canada will be represented at any such meetings, and that in line with our traditional position in these matters the Canadian government will give full and energetic support to this initiative. Our object is to reach an international understanding which will be fair to importing and exporting countries alike, and which will permit trade to expand without disruptive effects on our established industries.
A comprehensive international settlement will, of course, take time to accomplish. Meanwhile we shall continue to seek understandings on particular problems and with individual countries as we have in the case of Japan and Hong Kong. Needless to say, these international efforts are without prejudice to our rights under existing trade agreements to take measures where necessary to avoid injury to particular Canadian industries.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will have listened with interest to the statement which the Minister of Finance has just made, and I think also the house will have welcomed the statement in connection with the international conference to deal with this difficult, complex and varied question of textiles. It arises out of conditions which are not only national but international in scope and affect the United States, the United Kingdom and other countries all of which have a keen interest in the industry, and this makes the matter one of tremendous importance for Canada. Our country has a large number of textile industries, mostly in the central part of Canada but also in the other provinces, and everything that can be done to assist them will be welcomed on this side of the house.
I must say, however, that press comments on some of the statements that have been made by the Minister of Finance with respect to quotas and other matters have not been too favourable. That is why a conference of this nature is of the utmost importance. We on this side of the house will watch carefully and with keen interest what develops in this field from time to time.

Mr. Speaker, this group welcomes the interesting announcement made by the Minister of Finance. We are glad to know that Canada is co-operating in an effort to promote comprehensive understanding of this trade problem on an international basis. In our opinion consultation is the proper and logical course to follow. Our trade will benefit and therefore our people as well will benefit on the basis of an agreement reached as the result of international understanding on a most complicated and difficult problem.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fullon (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REVISION OF PROVISIONS RESPECTING DEATH PENALTY
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-92, to amend the Criminal Code (capital murder).
He said: Mr. Speaker, only on rare occasions is this house required to consider and amend or change laws or institutions that form part of the very foundation of our society. Such a task is to be undertaken today in the form of consideration of the advisability of amending the criminal law affecting the most heinous of crimes, murder. The bill now presented to the house represents the most progressive and far-reaching move in this field in Canada since we did away with public hanging. It may be remembered as a matter of interest that the last known case of such a hanging was the execution of the assassin of a former member of this house.
Before presenting an outline of the bill being introduced by the government, it may be helpful if I review briefly some of the history of the developments in the law on capital punishment in England, the United States and Canada, and give a general outline of the position taken by this government in its approach to the current problem in this country.
In the matter of capital punishment the criminal law of England, which of course we

inherited, has come a long way from its onetime harshness. It has been mentioned many times that 72,000 persons were executed for crime during the 38 years of the reign of Henry VIII. Tresham Lever, in his book, "The Life and Times of Sir Robert Peel", says that when Peel became home secretary there were more than 200 offences legally punishable with death.
A pickpocket, apprehended in the act, could, under the criminal law of England, suffer death for his crime; ... to cut down a tree, steal a fish . . . exposed one to the same punishment. Needless to say, the extreme penalty was seldom, if ever, exacted in cases of this sort, and the law was brought into contempt by juries refusing to convict on the plainest evidence of guilt.
The efforts of reformers such as Sir Samuel Romilly and Sir James Mackintosh to mitigate this formal severity were not very successful. Romilly did succeed in bringing about the repeal of two statutes of Elizabeth, one making it a capital offence to pick a person's pocket and the other making it a capital offence for a soldier or sailor to beg without a permit from his commanding officer or a local magistrate.
Professor Reckless in his book "Criminal Behaviour" points out that by 1839 a thousand bankers had softened enough to sign a petition presented to the House of Commons asking that the death penalty be eliminated as the punishment for forgery, but others have suggested that this was prompted less by any feeling of humanity than by the fact that juries were refusing to convict.
In 1866 a royal commission considered the abolition of capital punishment and recommended that there be two degrees of murder. This was not implemented by legislation, but in 1868 public executions were abolished by statute. It had been found that their effect was exactly the opposite of what was intended. Instead of being occasions of awful solemnity, they had become scenes of public debauchery.
Although bills were considered in the British House of Commons on matters relating to capital punishment in 1872, they were not passed. In 1931 a special committee was set up:
To consider the question of capital punishment in cases tried by civil courts in times of peace, and to report whether another penalty and if so of what nature should be substituted for the sentence of death in such cases where the sentence of death is now prescribed by law.
This committee proposed legislation to abolish the death penalty during an experimental period and also that, pending legislative action, there should be commutation in all cases. This committee's report was not acted on. In 1948 a member of the British House of Commons, Mr. Silverman, introduced
Criminal Code
an abolitionist bill. Clause 1 of the bill sought to suspend the death penalty for a period of five years. The bill was passed by the House of Commons but was overwhelmingly defeated by the House of Lords. The House of Commons then proposed a substitute for clause 1 to restrict the death penalty to five enumerated kinds of murder, the sentence in other cases to be imprisonment for life. This also was voted down by the House of Lords.
During the debate on the Silverman bill all sentences of death were commuted. As a result, in the weeks between April 16 and June 10, 1948, according to the royal commission on capital punishment known as the Gowers commission, "14 capital sentences were commuted and it is understood that in some ten of these cases reprieve probably would not have been granted in ordinary circumstances", report, pages 326-7. At the conclusion of the debate, the law on capital punishment remained in the position in which it stood prior to the bill, and the moratorium on hanging was lifted.
In 1949 the royal commission on capital punishment headed by Sir Ernest Gowers was set up having as its terms of reference:
-to consider and report whether liability under the criminal law in Great Britain to suffer capital punishment for murder should be limited or modified and, if so, to what extent and by what means, for how long and under what conditions persons who would otherwise have been liable to suffer capital punishment should be detained, and what changes in the existing law and the prison system would be required; and to inquire into and take account of the position in those countries whose experience and practice may throw light on these questions.
Its report was presented to parliament in the month of September of 1953, and it constitutes the most complete analysis of the question in modern times. The commission concluded that murder should not be redefined nor divided into degrees. It recommended against the proposal "that the judge should be empowered to substitute a lesser sentence for the sentence of death when a person is convicted of murder". The commissioners came to the conclusion, as reported in paragraph 551 of their report:
. .. that they would entrust to the jury, besides their primary and established functions of deciding whether an accused person charged with murder is guilty or innocent, the additional function of deciding, if he is guilty, whether a lesser punishment should be inflicted in lieu of the penalty of death.
In 1957 after further consideration the parliament of Great Britain passed an act entitled "The Homicide Act, 1957". This act adopted the approach of dividing murder into two classes, those which carry the death penalty and those for which the penalty is life imprisonment. The division, however, is based rather on the method or weapon by

Criminal Code
which the killing is accomplished, or in certain cases upon the person or class of person killed rather than on the nature and circumstances of the crime itself.
This has produced some arbitrary and rather unsatisfactory results. Thus, if a person kills another by shooting he is liable to the death penalty, whereas if he strangles or clubs him to death he may avoid that penalty although the latter crime may be more callous, brutal or premeditated than the former. We have sought to avoid this kind of result in making our division, as to the basis for which I shall have more to say later.
In the United States of America the application of the death penalty is, again according to the summary contained in the Gowers commission report, paragraphs 515 and 517, "limited by two methods, employed either separately or more often in combination. The first is the establishment of two or more degrees of murder; the second is a discretion to mitigate the sentence, usually conferred on the jury but vested in the court when the accused pleads guilty. Degrees of murder have not been established in approximately ten states...the definition of murder in the first degree is always derived from the definition in the Pennsylvania statute of 1794 which includes murders perpetrated by means of poison, or by lying in wait, or by any other kind of wilful, deliberate and premeditated killing and committed in the perpetration or attempt to perpetrate any arson, rape, robbery or burglary. The second degree usually includes all other murders".
In Canada attempts to alter the death penalty for murder began at least as far back as 1914, when Mr. Robert Bickerdike introduced bills to abolish capital punishment in several sessions of the House of Commons beginning in that year. Although they were debated at length, none of them resulted in legislation. In 1924 Mr. William Irvine introduced a similar bill which also failed of passage. In 1937 a bill was introduced by Mr. Blair to provide that the sentence of death be executed in a lethal chamber rather than by hanging. This bill was referred to a special committee which reported unfavourably on the proposal. In 1947 and again in 1950 the Canadian institute of public opinion made two inquiries with almost identical results, 68 per cent in favour of retaining capital punishment against 23 per cent in favour of life imprisonment.
In 1950 and again in 1952 Mr. Ross Thatcher introduced a bill to abolish capital punishment. On the latter occasion he withdrew it on the undertaking from the then minister of justice that at the next session parliament would be asked to set up a committee to go into the matter fully.

The most authoritative recent exposition in Canada has been the report of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on capital punishment, corporal punishment and lotteries which was set up pursuant to the undertaking referred to. This committee, which studied these matters for two years, in 1954 and 1955, recommended the retention of capital punishment, and in this respect the bill before the house meets the recommendation of the committee. The committee also recommended that there be no degrees of murder. In this respect the bill does not follow the recommendation of the joint committee.
The deep and continuing concern of hon. members with this subject is shown by the debates that took place both last year and this year on certain private members' bills. Although these debates took place on one bill only, a bill for the abolition of capital punishment for murder, the fact is that last year at least three bills were introduced all differing in their proposals. While these bills approached the subject from different directions, they did have in common an assumption of dissatisfaction with the present position and a desire to bring the law in this connection in closer conformity with present day concepts of crime and punishment.
I believe we owe much to the members who sponsored those bills, the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee), the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drys-dale) and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), quite apart from the question whether or not we agreed with their specific proposals. I believe the ensuing debate on this bill will be all the better for the thinking and formulation of ideas about this subject which those bills stimulated.
Although none of those bills was adopted, an analysis of the debates which took place, as well as discussions with those who did not participate, show quite clearly that the majority of members in the house favour retention of capital punishment. It became equally obvious, however, that even among those opposed to abolition there are serious misgivings as to the present law and practice governing the death penalty. It therefore seems proper and desirable to bring about some modification of that law and practice.
There is another thing which, in my submission, a review of these debates, as well as a study of all that has been said and written elsewhere, makes quite clear. It is that while the authorities are of some assistance and the debates have been of help, nevertheless this is an area where views are held with such depth of feeling that they are never going to be changed by mere weight of argument or

statistics. Indeed, on the question of the deterrent effect especially, statistics cannot give a satisfactory answer; there are no statistics of murders not committed. But as in the case of all such problems, there has to be some finality, responsibility has to be taken and a decision has to be made, and this the government has done.
We have accordingly approached the question on broad grounds. We have first been mindful of the fact that the criminal law must endeavour to translate into an enforceable code the highest concepts of the moral and legal standards by which society desires to be governed, while at the same time, since it must command respect if it is to achieve this purpose, it must broadly reflect the actual state of public opinion.
Second, we have taken account of the fact that the country, as reflected by opinion in this house, favours retention of capital punishment. Third, we have also recognized that even among those who favour retention there is a general feeling that the law should be modified. Finally, we have taken account of the feelings against the rather artificial division of murder into degrees based on the means by which it is committed or the class of person who is killed.
Thus while we have avoided the rather arbitrary and rigid classifications found in the British homicide act, we have put more emphasis on the element of deliberation as the requisite for capital murder than has been the case generally in the United States. We have also provided for an automatic review by the court of appeal, and for an appeal as of right to the Supreme Court of Canada. In short, we have applied our own thinking to the mass of authority and opinion available, and have produced a bill which represents our views of the kind of law by which Canadians would wish to be and should be governed. On this broad basis we take full responsibility for presenting this bill to the house.
Before coming to an outline of the bill itself I should say one other word about the decision to retain capital punishment. This decision does not rest on any one or narrow ground. With regard to the argument in favour of deterrent effect, the Gowers commission on capital punishment in the United Kingdom, which has been described as "the richest source of information, factual as well as impressionistic" on this subject, expressed the view "that there is some evidence, though no convincing statistical evidence, that the penalty of death is likely to have a stronger effect as a deterrent to normal human beings than any other form of punishment". That statement may be found in paragraph 68 of the report of that commission.
Criminal Code
Whatever strength or validity be ascribed to this view-and there is surely much to be said for it-is available therefore in support of this bill which retains capital punishment for a planned and deliberate murder or a murder committed in the course of a crime which generally speaking involves wilfulness or premeditation taken in the broad sense of those words.
But the general base on which it rests in so far as concerns the retention of capital punishment for deliberate murder, is this: That society requires for its preservation and protection that certain laws be observed. The whole basis of society, in the sense of any ordered form of life, would dissolve and chaos would reign if we did not have laws embodying that code of conduct by which, collectively, we say we desire to live. And because we live in an imperfect world, these laws require sanctions. Now, there are laws or rules of conduct of greater or lesser importance; therefore there are and must be sanctions of greater or lesser degree. But whatever be the sanction it is not a matter of retribution or revenge: It is an integral and essential element necessary to ensure the moral as well as the material vigour of the system of laws of which it is a part. If there is no sanction, the law ceases to have any effect.
Society's concern for its basic rules is expressed in its commands and corresponding sanctions that together constitute our criminal law. The degree of society's concern with respect to individual rules is reflected in the method of expression adopted.
In this sense, therefore, the sanction for the law against murder may properly reflect the importance which society attaches to the maintenance of that law. In our view, Canadians properly attach so high a value to the sanctity of human life that the law which translates this feeling into effective form should provide the maximum sanction for its deliberate breach, and no other penalty would be considered adequate.
This, Mr. Speaker, is perhaps only another way of saying that this bill reflects the view that Canadians are not prepared to accept the abolition, as distinguished from the restriction, of the death penalty. But it also reflects the feeling that it is not appropriate that the death penalty should be applicable automatically to every case of murder.
In carrying out the delicate but important task of bringing the law into line with our convictions in this field, we have concentrated our attention on producing a system which represents a rational and logical application of those principles of law upon which I have touched. We have accordingly started on the

Criminal Code
basis that there are two broad types of killing. The first is where the death does not result from any act of deliberation on the part of the person causing it but can be said to be impulsive or non-deliberate, in the sense of being in no way within the prior contemplation of that person. It is our view that the death penalty ought not to be the consequence in these cases, and accordingly although the crime may be murder, it is classed as non-capital and a sentence of life imprisonment only is provided.
The other type of killing is the case where death is caused deliberately or as the result of a planned act of the person causing it. All these cases are classed as capital murder and for these cases, but for these cases only, the sentence of death will follow automatically on conviction.
This type of case should, in our view, include two categories. The first is the case where the death results as a deliberate and planned end in itself. A killing was intended; the death penalty is automatically invoked. The second is the category in which, although a killing itself may not have been consciously and initially planned, yet the course of action embarked upon or planned had within it such an element of criminality and violence, as well as of deliberation or stealth, that the killing must properly be regarded as deliberate by the person who did it or who counselled or procured the doing of the act which caused it. This type of killing then, is also made to fall within the category of capital murder.
A very important and forward move is embodied in and results from this approach, with respect to the position of the accomplice. One of the very difficult and almost insoluble dilemmas with which juries and indeed the courts themselves have been confronted under the present law is that where two or more persons embark upon a joint criminal venture in the course of which one of them kills, the other or others, even though having had no direct or indirect participation in the precise act which caused the death, yet in law are guilty of murder and if convicted are automatically sentenced to death.
In our view no person, unless he actually causes a death or counsels or procures the act which causes it, should be liable to forfeit his own life. Accordingly this bill is so framed that the accomplice who did not actually cause the death, or counsel or procure the very act which caused the death, may still be found guilty of murder, but only of non-capital murder.
The house will appreciate that these results are accomplished without any disturbance of the existing law or jurisprudence which define homicide and murder and which define

liability in the case of the accomplice or the aider and abettor. The fact that it was homicide, that the homicide was culpable and that it was a culpable homicide constituting murder will all have to be established under the same provisions as are now applicable.
In other words, the killing will have to be shown to constitute murder. Only then, by this bill, the important and essential question is made to arise; is it capital murder or non-capital murder? By this bill the answer to that question is made to depend on the answer to another question; was the killing planned and deliberate or was it done in the course of committing another crime of a nature which the law holds to be such that it imports into the killing the element of deliberation? If the answer to that question is yes, then the murder is capital and the penalty is death; if the answer is no, the murder is non-capital and the penalty is life imprisonment.
It will also be appreciated that these questions are questions for the jury. But before the issue can arise at all the crown will have to decide whether it considers that the elements of capital murder are there; that is, whether the killing was planned and deliberate, and whether the crown can prove this. For the bill provides that if the accused is to be tried for capital murder he must be so charged in the indictment, and only if he is so charged can he be convicted of capital murder. If he is so charged, the jury may still decide that capital murder has not been proven and convict him of non-capital murder. They cannot convict of capital murder on a charge of non-capital murder.
So the onus is first on the crown to decide whether to charge capital or non-capital murder, and to prove the charge. On a charge of capital murder, then, it will be open to the jury to decide that the charge is proven and to convict accordingly, or to decide that it is non-capital murder and convict of that; or to decide, as they can now, that murder itself is not proved and in such case to convict of manslaughter or to acquit.
Juries, and indeed the whole administration of this branch of the criminal law will, I believe, be immeasurably assisted by this new approach. For whereas up to now juries have had to reach their verdict under the awful burden of knowledge that if they found the killing to be murder at all, then no matter what the extenuating circumstances might be the sentence of death was automatic; from now on they will know that the law itself takes formal account of the thousand and one different combinations of circumstances that may lead to or from the background of any such event which brings an accused before them on a charge of murder. It will only be

Criminal Code
if they his peers consider, after hearing all the evidence, that his crime of murder was planned and deliberate that they will convict him accordingly. If they do not so consider, or if they find that he did not commit the murder in the course of committing another crime which makes the killing in effect a planned and deliberate one, they may still convict him of murder if murder is proven, in the sure knowledge that he will not then be liable to the penalty which society itself feels should only be exacted for the most calculated and deliberate defiance of society's basic law.
Everyone who thinks about and discusses these matters is aware that juries have found it difficult almost to the point of impossibility to bring in a verdict of guilty where they know that, having regard to human feelings, human motives and human emotions, the death penalty would be unjust. In the result, the verdict is sometimes manslaughter although the facts are patently at variance with the verdict; or if a verdict of murder is brought in it is followed by such deep remorse or revulsion as to constitute a danger to the very jury system itself.
There are one or two other features of the bill which deserve special mention as matters of principle. The first is the automatic review by the court of appeal in the case where the death penalty has been imposed. This is another recognition of the desire of society to see an accused surrounded with every proper protection and to ensure that never can it be said that anyone met his death at the hands of the law for lack of funds. It is also a recognition of the fact that although to err is human, when a man is on trial for his life whatever precautions can be taken to avoid, or to correct, possible judicial or other error must be taken.
Next, we have provided as a new feature that wherever a verdict of guilty of capital murder has been rendered, the jury shall be asked if it has any recommendation to make. This is in recognition of the faot that there is an infinite variety of circumstances forming the background of motivation for human conduct, and many degrees of personal responsibility for and ability to control and answer for individual acts. It may well be, therefore, that although an accused was guilty of a deliberate killing, and did not come technically within one of the defences of provocation or insanity, the jury will still feel that the background of the case, or the circumstances of the accused's personality or mentality, were such that a recommendation should be made.
The provision will have another important result. At present judges and juries take differing views of the right of a jury to make any recommendation after verdict, the code being silent on the point. There have been some judges who have discouraged juries from making a recommendation, and jurymen have been known to say afterwards that if they had known they might make a recommendation they would certainly have done so. In the light of the seriousness that must inevitably attach to such a recommendation it seems to be essential that there should be a uniform practice regarding it, and we have provided one accordingly.
It is obvious from the form of question we have devised to be put to the jury at this stage, that there will be an important connection between the views of the jury in this regard and the system of executive review of cases where the death penalty has been imposed, upon which the exercise of mercy is based. The bill makes no change in that system, which we intend should be preserved.
I should like to emphasize only two things about that system, which I think have been misunderstood. The first is that it does not constitute any sort of review or reversal of the jury's verdict or the judge's sentence. The trial is over, and jury and judge have rendered their verdict and pronounced sentence as provided by law. But now that same law says to the cabinet, you now have the duty of examining all aspects of the case, including those that may not have been before the court, to see whether for any reason clemency should be shown, or whether the sentence in this case should be carried out.
The other feature is this. Although the making or withholding of a recommendation is and will continue to be of very real import, the discretion of the executive as to the advice it tenders to His Excellency is unfettered. It is not a question of determining again the guilt or innocence of the condemned man according to law; it is a system in which the law imposes upon the cabinet at the ultimate stage the duty of determining whether in this individual case the law should take its course. It is a solemn and an extremely difficult task, but it is a feature of our system which gives assurance of the preservation of an essential feature of any system of justice: that it shall be tempered with mercy.
We submit this bill, then, Mr. Speaker, in the belief that the protection of society demands that one who deliberately commits murder should be liable to the death penalty, and that this reflects the views and demands

Criminal Code
of Canadian society. It reflects also our belief that the law should not provide the death penalty for every murder, but only for those which have about them the element of deliberation; and we believe that this also reflects the proper judgment and demand of our society.
Finally, we present it in the conviction that in its merciful and progressive provision of an age limit below which no one shall be executed, and of an automatic review by an appeal tribunal to remove so far as possible the element of human or judicial error, together with its other progressive features, it represents a proper reconciliation between the necessity for the protection of the lives of decent and law-abiding citizens on the one hand, and the desire of a Christian and civilized society to see justice tempered with mercy and forbearance on the other. On this basis we submit it for the approval of the house.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that all hon. members listened with great interest to the statement of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton).
Right at the beginning of his remarks, the minister reminded us that only on rare occasions is the house required to consider such a significant bill as it affects the very life of the citizen. It was, indeed, from that point of view that last Saturday I asked, or rather tried to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) whether hon. members opposite would take an entirely personal attitude in the discussion of this bill, discounting all political considerations as party members, as we were invited to do last year, when a similar bill was discussed.
As far as I am concerned, the remarks I shall make are of a strictly personal order and I trust that hon. members opposite will do the same, so that our fellow citizens will know our remarks and the vote we will cast as the expression of our own personal opinion.
Mr. Speaker, since 1957 there have been,
I think, in Canada about ten executions following a death sentence pronounced by our courts, whereas in 39 other cases, where the indicted person had been condemned to death, the royal mercy was exercised to commute the sentence. Such a situation was obviously unusual. And last year, when I expressed my views on a bill which is somehow connected with the subject, I said that we had now in Canada a partial abolition of

capital punishment because of a massive commutation of sentences, for I think that, after initiating such course in numerous cases, the cabinet can hardly refuse the commutation of his sentence to any individual in a case where a crime had been committed under similar circumstances. It is therefore high time for the government to adopt a definite position and assume its responsibilities by submitting a bill to regularize a situation which the government iself created.
Bill C-92 provides in the definition of murder various degrees of guilt and punishment. We shall have an opportunity of fully discussing the bill in committee. It may be that several members will, at that time, suggest significant amendments, because I must admit for my part that the terms of various sections of the bill do not seem quite clear to me, and, to my mind, some improvements might very well be suggested. However, as we are now on second reading, I shall at this time discuss the principle of the bill submitted by the government and the Minister of Justice.
But before doing so, I think it would be interesting to recall some recommendations contained in the report of the joint committee of the Senate and this house on capital punishment, which was submitted on June 27, 1956. And after having read some of those recommendations, we will see that the government took it upon itself to submit to us today various amendments which are the complete opposite of the committee's suggestions.
Section 95 on page 23 of the report deals with the recommendations of the committee.
One of those is the retention of capital punishment as mandatory penalty for murder.
Briefly here is what the committee had to say on that point. I am now quoting section 63 on page 16:
While the committee considered that capital punishment should be subjected to periodic review by parliament, it recommends that the death penalty should be retained as the mandatory punishment for the crime of murder.
We now come to the second recommendation. The definition of murder remains unchanged. Section 69, on page 17 of the report, reads as follows:
In practice, the committee considered that any redefinition of the crime of murder should conform closely to the present practice in commuting sentences of capital punishment. Having concluded that it is not practicable to achieve a satisfactory redefinition of murder, the committee also decided that differences between murders can only be recognized by granting commutation in suitable circumstances. Since differentiation in the crime of murder depends to a considerable extent upon the assessment of moral culpability of a crime,

the committee is of the opinion that the ends of justice are best served by the continuation of the present practice of mitigating the rigour of the law in appropriate cases by the exercise of executive clemency.
Several witnesses suggested that consideration might be given to the creation of degrees of murder which would take into account the difference in moral culpability between different types of homicides. All witnesses representing law-enforcement authorities opposed the establishment of degrees of murder. The committee shares the conclusions of the United Kingdom royal commission on this question. The committee is of the opinion that the present distinction between murder and manslaughter is quite clear and straightforward. It considers that any attempt to break murder down into degrees may lead to the creation of technical and confusing distinctions without, at the same time, creating any precise delineation between murders of differing degrees of moral culpability.
I should also like to refer to another section of these recommendations; it deals with the abolition of hanging and its replacement by electrocution or, as an alternative, by the gas chamber.
I refer to section 91 of that report, on page 21. Here is what the committee had to say:
The committee considered that one of the principal objections to hanging was that so much depended upon the personal competence of the hangman, leaving a greater margin for error than in the case of execution by electrocution or the gas chamber. It may be that a hanging, conducted efficiently and with proper facilities, may be accomplished more quickly and with less anguish to the condemned person than the other two methods of execution. The committee noted that, for this reason, the United Kingdom royal commission concluded that hanging should be retained. The evidence of medical witnesses and others, however, indicated that hangings in Canada were not conducted with the same degree of precision as in the United Kingdom and that there was no way of knowing, in some cases, how death was caused and whether loss of consciousness had been instantaneous. Examples of bungled hangings were brought to the committee's attention. Moreover, the committee sensed from the evidence given by experienced officials and others, that hanging was regarded generally as being an obsolete, if not a barbaric, method of execution. The committee has concluded, after weighing these considerations, that hanging is not the most satisfactory method of execution which might be employed and, accordingly, recommends its abolition.
Mr. Speaker, I certainly think this committee which sat for two sessions-I think it was in 1955 and 1956-and considered the recommendations and views of various experts on the matter, I even think the executioner was heard, submitted a worth-while report, based on a very thorough study of the technical aspects.
I therefore wonder why the various aspects of this bill run counter to the report of that committee. I wonder why the government has not seen fit to follow much more closely the recommendations in that report.
Criminal Code
However, the government has taken the initiative and responsibility of this bill and now asks us to approve new definitions of the crime of murder. Thus this bill attempts to draw a distinction on the basis of premeditation, which will make the crime capital murder, whereas in cases where premeditation cannot be established, it will be non-capital murder.
After listening a moment ago to the Minister of Justice, 1 believe that we are now putting a heavy burden on the shoulders of the provincial attorneys general by leaving them with the responsibility of determining what a charge they will be called upon to lay against an accused.
As the minister pointed out, an indictment of non-capital murder is laid against an individual, and during the hearing of the case it becomes obvious that a capital murder is involved, it will then be impossible to convict that accused of a capital murder.
The case would be different if a charge of capital murder were laid and the evidence pointed to circumstances indicating that there had been no premeditation. Then if my assumption is right a verdict of non capital murder would be rendered.
I am under the impression that we are imposing quite a responsibility on the jury. I think that all those who have some court experience will agree-and experience points in that direction-that juries feel repugnance against the death penalty and are loath to make a decision which could send a man to his death. That is why in many instances in recent years, juries have rendered verdicts inconsistent with the evidence, simply because they felt reluctant to making such a decision-and this is a human reaction for men with no court experience-and did not want to assume responsibility for a decision which would have involved loss of life for one of their fellow men.
I would have hoped that this bill instead of giving the jury more responsibility would have reduced it. Last year in our debate on that matter, I expressed the opinion that in cases where human life is at stake, we should refer to a bench of three judges instead of a jury.
I definitely think that even though the principle of the bill is justified, the implementation of that piece of legislation by juries across the land will not do justice to it and that as a rule verdicts of non-capital murder will be returned.

Criminal Code
Now, this distinction between a capital and a non-capital murder, based on premeditation, is a legal concept.
We are here in a very restricted field. I believe that the minister would admit, if he were to review the 39 cases in which the government saw fit to exercise the royal mercy, that in most of those cases, it was capital murder, where there was evidence of premeditation.
This bill is based on a distinction which is actually a legal concept. I wonder whether in practice, this bill will answer the purpose that the government had in mind in drafting it. Therefore, I ask the minister whether in his opinion-I shall take his word for it-in most of those 39 cases where royal mercy was exercised, there was an element of premeditation and whether those cases met the definition of capital murder contained in Bill C-92?
I feel the government intended to reserve capital punishment for the most odious and serious murders and to see that a life sentence be given in the other cases. Besides, that was the opinion I expressed last year.
I wonder if the terms of this bill lead us directly to the enactment of the underlying principle of this bill?
Up to now, the differentiation of responsibility in murder cases was quite clear and unequivocal about murder, as defined under section 202, and manslaughter. After reading and re-reading the terms of this bill, I feel that if we adopt this measure in its context, as it is submitted today, the bill might become a picnic for learned and clever lawyers. I think that, should the bill be adopted in its present form and context, it would mean, for all practical purposes, almost complete abolition of capital punishment in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I hope you will allow me to deal very briefly with a question I asked about two weeks ago to the Minister of Justice, which was indirectly related to this bill.
The legislators' intention is and must be first of all to prevent crime, to make it more difficult to commit. The minister is aware that we asked him last year, and again this year, whether the government intended to introduce an amendment to the Criminal Code in order to establish an exceedingly strict control over the possession and use of firearms.
It is that use of firearms which today leads us directly to discussing the definition of

murder, and I recognize that I am very sorry that the government never thought it worth while to submit in the current session, a bill which would make the ownership of firearms extremely difficult.
Today, people who have very bad police records may go about armed in our streets, and the minister knows, while experience proves, that penalties provided in those cases are extremely slight. I would hope that the government will soon submit legislation with regard to the possession of firearms, and I even expected that such a bill would have preceded the legislation we are now discussing, which deals with an amendment to clause 202 of the Criminal Code.
Incidentally, I want to congratulate the authorities of the province of Quebec, who, in nine cases out of ten this year, refused to renew firearms permits. I sincerely hope that the attorneys general of the other provinces will do the same and that, during the next session of parliament, some stricter legislation with regard to owning firearms will be submitted to us by the federal Minister of Justice.
Mr. Speaker, earlier I read a recommendation by the joint committee with regard to the method of execution, and I do not quite understand why the government did not today choose to carry out that recommendation which declared hanging an obsolete and barbarous method of execution.
The minister himself reminded us at the beginning of his remarks, that such questions are not submitted to parliament every day. I think it would have been wise to accept that recommendation. I submit that before we pass to the discussion of the articles of the bill in the committee of the whole, I think there is still time for the government to revise its attitude in this respect. Indeed, if I do not deceive myself, I do not think the minister mentioned the mode of execution nor did he tell us why the government is not ready to carry out such a serious recommendation which is the result of intensive study by experts who gave their help to the members of the joint committee.
And now, Mr. Speaker, let me say just a few words with regard to the absence of any provisions in the case of women. I do not know whether it is out of natural weakness-indeed I do not exactly know how to explain that attitude-but I would like to see women exempt from capital punishment and provision in the statutes for life imprisonment in the case of any woman having committed capital murder.

Women have been very rarely executed in Canada. As a matter of fact, for the past ten years or so, there has been no such execution, as far as I know. Indeed, experience has shown that murders committed by women were accompanied by very special circumstances, and even if the committee placed women on equal footing with men, with regard to capital punishment, I wonder whether, in the case of women, an exemption would not be in harmony with the view of society today. At any event, I do not believe that a woman is ever executed, except in quite unforeseen circumstances.
Mr. Chairman, I should also like the minister to explain the meaning of life imprisonment. When an individual has been sentenced to life imprisonment, will the rehabilitation board-

Mr. Speaker, I should also like to make a few comments on clause 13 of this bill, but, before doing so, may I be permitted to read the clause in question:
Where a jury finds an accused guilty of an offence punishable by death, the judge who presides at the trial shall, before discharging the jury, put to them the following question:
You have found the accused guilty and the law requires that I now pronounce sentence of death against him (or "the law provides that he may be sentenced to death", as the case may be). Do you wish to make any recommendation as to whether or not he should be granted clemency. You are not required to make any recommendation, but if you do make a recommendation either in favour of clemency or against it, your recommendation will be included in the report that I am required to make of this case to the Minister of Justice and will be given due consideration.
I do not think that such a recommendation is practical. I said a moment ago that juries would naturally feel reluctant to convict a man of an offence punishable by death.
Well, when the jury has taken its responsibility and decided that it is, in its opinion, a capital murder, and when it has returned a verdict to that effect, I wonder why a judge should have to ask the jury whether or not it should recommend mercy towards the accused. I fail to see the use of such a recommendation and I think that it rather contradicts the definition of a capital murder.
One must be realistic in such matters. If the jury is given the clear evidence of a premeditated murder, in circumstances indicated in the bill now before us, why then ask that jury to recommend mercy?
Criminal Code
Why not let another judicial body decide whether mercy could be exercised in such and such a case, depending upon the circumstances of the case?
I do hope that the minister will elaborate a little on this subject because I think that a responsibility is being placed upon the jury which it will not be able to refuse. A jury may return a verdict of guilty compelling the judge to pass death on the accused. This jury will not be ready to say: I am against recommending the accused to the mercy of the court. There is nothing logical nor practical in this situation; at least, I fail to see its practical meaning.
Now, Mr. Speaker, with such a bill, time only will tell whether it meets the intent of the government.
I should say that on the whole, this bill is legally justifiable, but in practice and I say that its enforcement will go far beyond the intent of the government.
The minister did not tell us whether the government had consulted the Canadian bar association before introducing this bill. In view of the importance it will have and the questions it should raise in the mind of every hon. member who will rise in this debate, I wonder whether it would not be wise, when the bill reaches a certain stage of the procedure, possibly after its consideration in committee, to put off its passing until another session in order to give the public time to reach a decision and to provide for bodies such as the Canadian Bar Association an opportunity to make their views known.
May I ask you to call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Justice has introduced today a most important bill. All bills, of course, are important, but this one is of particular importance because it concerns statutory provisions relating to the life or death or imprisonment for life of those charged with the most heinous, vicious crime of homicide.
Today, sir, in considering this legislation we are deciding whether the penalty for this crime shall be life imprisonment or death. I

Criminal Code
know we all appreciate very much the introduction to this bill by the minister, and the pains he took to give us an historical background of the penal laws of the United Kingdom, the United States of America and Canada as they related to the crime of homicide and the penalty for it. I think we owe a debt of gratitude to the minister for having given us this historical background and for following it up with an explanation of the basis upon which the government arrived at certain conclusions in introducing Bill No. C-92 which is now before us.
I, sir, cannot completely agree with all the conclusions that have been reached by the minister as he expressed them this morning. Nor can I agree to any extent with the opinions expressed by the previous speaker, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont. I noticed that both the Minister of Justice and the previous speaker made some reference to the findings and recommendations of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons which met for some two years. Any reference which I make to this joint committee will be to the record of information contained in the committee report and the transcript of evidence, some 1,665 pages, found in the two volumes I have on my desk at the moment.
May I say first of all, Mr. Speaker, that my own position is very well known. I have been interested in this question of capital punishment for some 25 years, and have reached certain conclusions. My decisions are not based on any emotionalism whatever. My decisions have been arrived at as a result of the fullest possible study I could make of everything on this subject in this country and throughout the world; a reading of the reports of royal commissions, parliamentary committees that have looked into the matter, and so on. Having concluded this study, I stand here this afternoon as I have on previous occasions, believing that the right thing to do is to abolish capital punishment. In saying that, sir, I do want to give credit to the Minister of Justice for having introduced Bill No. C-92, which is without doubt one of the first, and therefore one of the most progressive, approaches made toward this subject for many years.
In his interesting introduction to the bill this morning the minister, in my estimation, glossed over the information available throughout the world and the information available to the Senate and House of Commons joint committee as to whether capital punishment should be retained or abolished. I recognized what the Minister of Justice was

doing, but I should like to carry on and perhaps exercise my right to oppose the conclusion to which he came.
This morning the minister told us we could not accept the position that capital punishment was not a deterrent because we had no way of knowing how many homicides had not been committed because there is capital punishment. This is an extraordinary approach, in my opinion. I believe what we have to go by is the record throughout the world, so far as it can be examined and understood, relating to whether or not capital punishment is a deterrent to homicide.
As a result of 25 years of study, but in particular as a result of the evidence that was submitted to the joint committee which met for a period of over two years, it is my definite opinion that capital punishment is not a deterrent to homicide. I would suggest to the hon. member a study of the evidence placed before that joint committee, which had the advantage of presentations and advice from experts around the world who are interested in this matter and to which was submitted evidence, which I maintain is conclusive, that a study of the states or the countries which have or which have not capital punishment does not give in any way whatsoever an indication, in the ratio of homicides, that the retention of capital punishment is a deterrent to homicide.
It is not my intention to go into detail. However, I would draw to the attention of hon. members of this house that there are some countries which retain capital punishment and which have a very high ratio of homicides per 100,000 of population, and that there are others which retain capital punishment and which have a very low ratio of homicides. From the figures given to us in that committee we find that in El Salvador the ratio of homicides is 44.3 per 100,000 population, while in the United Kingdom in the same year the ratio was 0.5.
We have those countries which abolished the death penalty, some of them almost 100 years ago. We find that some countries which abolished the death penalty have a high ratio of homicides, and we find that others which abolished the death penalty have a very low ratio of homicides. The one with the highest ratio we were given was Colombia with 15.9 homicides per 100,000 of population, as compared with the Netherlands with 0.4 and Norway with 0.5, a figure almost identical with that for the United Kingdom.
I could, of course mention other countries and their ratios. However, the point I want

to make is this, and the evidence is there tor any who wants to read it. Whether a country is abolitionist or non-abolitionist, whether you have the death penalty or do not have it, the record of the world is that this fact does not have a relation to the rate of homicide of any comparative nature so that it can be differentiated as between the two policies.
I think perhaps one of the greatest comparative studies that can be made of this matter as a deterrent to homicide is with respect to those states in the United States which previously had capital punishment and then went to the abolition of capital punishment. Some stayed in that position, but some went back to capital punishment. I submit that from a study of that situation where they had it, got rid of it and went back to it; or had it, abolished it and did not go back to it, the ratio of differentiation between having it and not having it shows that the death penalty is not a deterrent to homicide.
I have often received letters and in previous sessions have often heard members speak in this house to this effect, saying that we must retain capital punishment or the death sentence because it is a protection for the police forces. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, only one factual study in the world has ever been made on this matter. I spoke about it, I believe either at the last session or the one previous. I refer to the study made in the United States by one of the top penologists of the world, using all his upper graduates. They made an investigation of every city of over 10,000 in the United States over a period of years. What was the answer? The answer was-and it was sent to our joint committee-that they could not find any comparable differentiation whether or not capital punishment was the law of the state, or that it made any difference with regard to the number of policemen who were killed. The ratio was almost identical, going up or down.
If any evidence could be produced in any manner whatsoever which would show that capital punishment is a deterrent to homicide or is a protection of our police forces, that would be good and solid ground for the retention by Canada of the death penalty for homicide. However, I submit that the record in all aspects in the United States, in varying states, and throughout the world does not demonstrate the correctness of either of those two arguments.
If therefore my contention and my analysis are correct, then why should we retain in any way whatsoever the death penalty? It can only be from prejudice, revenge, or the Mosaic law which demands an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth and a life for a life. Certainly in Canada in this modern age, in a Christian country, any argument based on
Criminal Code
prejudice, revenge or the Mosaic law is not something which we should consider in deciding whether to retain or abolish the death penalty.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, I have been interested in this subject for some 25 years. I venture to say that I have received more letters of commendation and condemnation than perhaps most other members. Those who oppose the abolition of the death penalty have one great argument, namely that because of the suffering of the relatives and friends of the victim, there should be suffering by the relatives and friends of the one who committed that homicide. You would be amazed, Mr. Speaker, if you knew how many letters I have received to that effect over this period of years.
Of course we all recognize the agonizing moments and the suffering of the relatives and friends of the victim of a homicide, and we sympathize with them. They are completely innocent; but they are made the victims because of the aberration, the impulse or the viciousness of somebody who committed murder. However, Mr. Speaker, they are innocent victims. I fail to understand why other innocent people, the relatives and friends of the one who committed the murder, should also suffer. I fail to understand why it is a reasonable answer that they too must suffer. Surely we have a more Christian, more idealistic, more scientific approach than that.
I have read Bill No. C-92, which is now before us, very carefully. I have noticed the emphasis placed by the minister on the differentiation between premeditated murder, which will carry the death penalty, and homicide committed as a result of emotion or impulse, which will be non-capital murder. The reason I mention this is because of the interest of the Prime Minister in this matter, as is shown by his presence here at this moment.
I admit that my interest is strictly academic, upon which I am going to speak only briefly. However, when I listened to the Minister of Justice speak about premeditated murder I could not help thinking, is it not also premeditated murder to sentence a man to death and carry out that sentence? I suppose the differentiation is that one is the murder of an individual and the other is death by order of society.
Of course I understand this differentiation, but basically is it justifiable? Is it justifiable to say that society can murder but an individual cannot? As I have said, it is just a question of academic interest, but I raise this matter also because the Prime Minister is here and has shown his interest in these matters by initiating the bill of rights. In

Criminal Code
the bill of rights there is the principle that no one in Canada shall suffer agonizing torture. I wonder whether hon. members realize the agonizing torture endured by a man who has been sentenced to death and who knows he is going to be executed. I have met and spoken to men in the death cell, and there certainly is agonizing torture on their part. They know their days are coming to an end. However, as I pointed out, these are questions of only academic concern, but I say they are of academic interest. That is all I am going to say about that aspect of the matter.
I do wish to now raise something which was not mentioned by the Minister of Justice or the previous speaker, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont. I refer to the fact that death is irrevocable. Why do we in Canada and in this government take the position that we are absolutely infallible, that we cannot make mistakes? I know the record is that we do not know whether or not we have ever made a mistake, but that is because nobody has had an interest in finding out whether a man was innocent after he was dead. I was most interested about two weeks ago in watching the rebroadcast of a half hour television program that was made in the United Kingdom. In that program a former home secretary, the head of the judiciary in that country, and two members of parliament stated they were afraid they had to admit that innocent people may have been hung in the United Kingdom. Death is irrevocable.
We have noted a similar situation in the United States, where it has been proven that a mistake has been made, and it has not just been a suspicion of a mistake. How many hon. members have read the reports of the final court of appeal, the court of last resort, whereby it has been conclusively proven on at least one occasion and I think on two that a man sentenced to death for homicide and whose sentence had been commuted to life imprisonment was not guilty at all, and he was released.
Apart from the court of last resort I was interested in reading only two weeks ago a report emanating from the United States concerning a man who had been found guilty of murder. It was said that he was guilty and there was no question about it. He was sentenced to death. The death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment and he had been in prison for ten years. Then a man admitted that he had committed the murder and the man who was in prison was innocent. An investigation by the authorities conclusively proved that the man who confessed was not a nut. The investigation proved that he had committed the homicide for which another

man had been found guilty and sentenced to death. This man had the death sentence commuted to life imprisonment, and after being in prison for ten years was released. But death is irrevocable. Are we, sir, infallible? I think this is a point which should be very seriously considered.
There is another point which I find of interest. I want to mention it because I must admit that I have not yet been able to make up my mind about it. There is a section in this act which the Minister of Justice very clearly explained, and I understand his explanation. The section deals with a jury which has convicted a person charged with capital murder, and provides that the judge must ask the jury whether they have anything to say; that is, whether they have any recommendation to make as far as mercy is concerned. I want it to be clearly understood that this is one aspect of this bill upon which at the moment I have not been able to make up my mind.
The crown lays the charge in the case of capital murder. The jury has to decide the case. The jury decides it. That is a terrible thing to have to do, but they must do it under our understanding of justice. The jury must decide whether the man or woman charged with capital murder is guilty, and capital murder carries the penalty of death. Then the judge must say to the jury, "Have you anything to say with regard to clemency, mercy or extenuating circumstances?" There we have a request of the jury which has already had to do something which a person does not like doing; that is, they have had to find a person guilty and see him sentenced to death. Then the jury is asked, "Shall the man die or shall he live?", because the judge says to them, "what you have to say will be conveyed to the Minister of Justice and through him to the Solicitor General", and then I presume to the cabinet which will decide whether or not there shall be exercised the Queen's prerogative of mercy.
I presume that because of the changes incorporated in this bill which we are now con-cidering, if for capital murder there were no recommendation for mercy it would be the majority thinking that the person should die. But if there is a recommendation from the jury with regard to that capital homicide, I should think, from experience of these past four years with this government, that there would be the commutation to life imprisonment through the exercise by the cabinet of the prerogative of mercy of the Queen.
Therefore basically I think the jury is actually being asked-they have found a person guilty of capital murder for which the sentence is death-to say what the penalty should be. I say, sir, that I find it rather

difficult to reach a conclusion as to whether that should be done. On balance I think perhaps it should be done, because of what I have just said; that if there is not that statement by the jury then in all probability the death penalty will be carried out. This is something upon which I should very much like to hear comments from the minister and other hon. members of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to deal with a subject which is upsetting to me. I have, of course, always wanted to see the death penalty abolished. However, if it is to be maintained, I should then ask what the method of execution is to be. This subject has been dealt with at some length by previous speakers and I should now like to make some further comments in this regard as well. Apparently the government, in its wisdom, has seen fit to retain the death penalty under certain circumstances. Should this house agree with that retention, surely in the interests of society it should be carried out in the most humane way possible. It is obvious from what has been said by the minister and previous speakers, as well as from the omission of any reference to the subject of the bill itself, that hanging is to be the method followed.

I suggest this is the first major step forward that has been taken in this country toward a stage of decency when the laws of society will be applied to protect society without the necessity of taking human life.

The very fact that the House of Commons and ultimately parliament, I hope, has recognized this principle will mean that it will be accepted in the minds of members of the cabinet that such a recommendation should be given some consideration.
I had the experience many years ago of defending a young boy who was 19 years old when he was tried. He had lived a sheltered and happy life with his mother. He had never been away from home. He lived on a farm, and whenever there was any of the usual slaughtering of animals to be done he so disliked the thought of blood being shed that he would absent himself from the farm on such occasions. On one occasion when he was 18 he left the farm and in a period of four days committed five grave breaches of the Criminal Code, including murder, under circumstances for which there could be no possible defence. The only defence I attempted to introduce was that of insanity. It was established that he had the mentality of a boy 10 or 11, but he could not be brought within the four corners of the narrow, legal definition of insanity which would have meant that there could have been a finding of not guilty.
He was found guilty, and I recall the sentence well. The case was heard in a frontier town in a theatre filled with people. When it was time for sentence to be passed the boy was sobbing. He was held up by policemen on either side as the judge pronounced the sentence of death. I remember speaking to him as he went away and assuring him that I would petition for commutation. The jury intimated to me afterward that they would have liked to bring in a recommendation for mercy. They felt they could not do other than find him guilty on the strength of the charge made by the

learned trial judge, but they certainly believed that there were circumstances with respect to the boy's background and mental condition which indicated to them that his life should not be taken. But because that was not done the sentence was carried out, and it was one case where I felt that the death penalty never should have been carried out.
It is in circumstances of that kind that clause 13 may well come into effect. I hope what I have said will to some extent resolve the doubts of the hon. member for Vancouver East, and that the important and forward looking clauses of the bill will receive the commendation of the house.
